I would like to point out that disk space took a hit when we all wanted to move to SSDs. The drive I have my games installed on is only 500G which is only twice as big as the drives I had 10 years ago (and my OS drive is only 120G).

I don't like "oversized" games because I think devs are lazy and just can't be bothered to try to make them smaller, like sofware devs don't care about CPU and RAM use in their programs so use Electron to write it. They all think we have nearly limitless resources to download and run their software so they don't have to care about size or performance. Okay for a video game you might trade disk space for CPU time, use uncompressed assets so you don't have to spend time decompressing them when you want them.

One concrete example I know of: Civilization V. It has (or had) 5 copies of the opening cinematic. The video stream was the same but it had different voice overs (English and 4 other European languages IIRC). They should have separated the audio from the video or put several language tracks in the same file.

The subject of SSDs is something that I intentionally left out. I don't disagree with what you say at all. Indeed, I think Internet distribution has lifted the physical size barriers than discs presented, and as a result packing a game down becomes "less important." I don't think the performance analogy quite fits this scenario. If games weren't performant (as seen on so many PC ports of console games) I would see that as a big problem. Still, even in cases where all the localization content is left in a game that the bulk of the size is still the game payload. Textures, models, cinematics, and sound all continue to become higher quality, but textures most of all, I think, are what is contributing most to game size.

There are a lot of things that can cut down size, but that doesn't necessarily mean that current sizes is a problem.

Let me ignore these parts of the game and cut down the size, this does not require a great deal of effort simply packaging the game in different chunks that are optional what you download.

You could also compress the files for download and let the person on the other end decompress them as part of the install process, or again make this an option to get the file heavily compressed and knowing that it would extend the install to decompress it.

Any options for reducing download size means that the company hosting the file can also decrease their bandwidth as they will have less data going over their network. giving us options my increase disc space for them but is a once and one expense unlike the internet connection that is monthly.

In regards to data-caps you are correct if you can get a nice 20megabit connection it is likely a terabyte. but some are on much more limited connections and with those come caps more like what you used to have with comcast and charter. However, as best I can tell from game repacks, most of the size reductions comes from using a different compression algorithm. I don't know why game distribution companies don't use something better. Install times, maybe? Regardless, it's not a new phenomenon. Game repacks have been around for just about as long as torrenting itself.

And regarding data caps, again I come back to my analogy with 4G. There are probably far more places without 4G coverage than there are with unreasonably small data caps. But it's always been a tug of war. Web pages get larger, apps get larger, games get larger . All of these things, too, could be made smaller in a lot of cases, and could be made to better suit areas with slow or capped speeds, but they are edge cases.
